source_title: A brief history of Quiznos' collapse
company_context: Quiznos was a toasted-sandwich QSR franchise that peaked at roughly 5,000 U.S. locations in the mid-2000s, then collapsed. Its franchisees (independent small-business owners) were squeezed by a corporate supply model and a debt-laden leveraged buyout, leading to mass closures and a 2014 Chapter 11.
macro_context: Great Recession demand pressure on QSR, intense competition from Subway, and a private-equity leveraged-buyout debt structure that loaded the parent with obligations.
evidence_summary: Quiznos' parent took on heavy LBO debt (a 2006 CCMP Capital buyout reportedly added ~$600 million in debt, refinanced up to ~$800 million, and total loan obligations reached ~$875 million by the 2014 filing). The franchise model required franchisees to buy supplies through a corporate distributor at above-market markups (~6-7%), so the parent profited from supply sales more than royalties while franchisee unit economics were crushed. U.S. locations fell from roughly 4,700 in 2007 to fewer than 400 by 2017; thousands of franchisees joined fraud/antitrust/racketeering litigation. Quiznos filed Chapter 11 in the District of Colorado on March 14, 2014.

source_backed_metrics.chapter_11_venue: U.S. Bankruptcy Court, District of Colorado

owner_decision_context: Corporate leadership (under PE ownership) chose to monetize franchisees through forced above-market supply purchases rather than profitable royalty growth, while servicing LBO debt. This destroyed franchisee profitability and trust; franchisees (small-business owners) closed units en masse or litigated.
action_taken: Maintained the high-markup captive-supply model and debt load; eventually filed Chapter 11 in 2014 and shed the vast majority of locations; settlements across franchise litigation were estimated at over $200 million.
outcome_evidence: Location count collapsed from ~4,700 (2007) to <400 (2017), Chapter 11 filed 2014-03-14 with ~$875M obligations, and large franchisee litigation - confirming a debt-plus-franchisee-economics failure ending in bankruptcy.
source_limitations: Primary trade-journalism source (Restaurant Business); WebFetch not used for full text. Figures corroborated across multiple outlets and Wikipedia in search snippets but are journalist-reported, not from a primary filing. Settlement totals and some debt figures are reported estimates. This is a secondary/named-journalism source, not a court docket.

Tests whether the engine separates parent-level debt/solvency pressure from franchisee-level unit-economics destruction and models the human/governance dimension (owner non-compliance, accountability, trust breakdown across a franchise network).
